introduction:
Hung Shui Kiu / Ha Tsuen (HSK/HT) is one of Hong Kong's largest new development areas, and the three-dimensional planning sandbox built for it must do more than display maps: it must let a planner **see what a design choice does**. When a user raises a block, plants a grove, strips a podium or lays a flood-storage basin, the sandbox should show the consequence for urban heat and for drainage, with ventilation as the coupled third axis. This report is a progress document: it records how those three screens are built, what each can and cannot claim, and the deterministic roadmap that carries them from prototype to testable product.

The organising finding is that heat, wind and drainage are not three features but **one geometry read three ways**. The research behind Hong Kong's Air Ventilation Assessment (AVA) framework states the design problem in a single sentence: a designer can “maximize wind speed and minimize solar radiation” to achieve comfort in the hot, humid Hong Kong summer ([Ng & Cheng, 2009](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0360132308001455)). Those are the only two variables a designer controls, and both are functions of the same massing — height, spacing, orientation, podium coverage and ground-level permeability. Because the runoff-generation term reads that same footprint-and-height raster, one scenario model can drive all three axes; building three separate models would encode the same geometry three times and let the three answers silently disagree.

The constraints are hard. The tool must run in pure **numpy + pillow + scipy** — no GDAL, no Docker, no GPU, no CFD — deterministically, in seconds on a laptop, so that the sandbox stays interactive. Under those constraints no screen may claim more than it can prove, and every number carries a screening-level honesty label; the label is a deliverable, not a footnote.

The report proceeds in five chapters. Chapter 1 turns an inert, hand-authored land-class tint into a design-responsive sky-view-factor and shadow screen anchored to a published Landsat LST or HKO normal. Chapter 2 breaks the wind screen's exact NE≡SW symmetry — fatal, because the published prevailing wind at HSK is NE/ENE/E, together 40.8% of the year ([AVRG73, PlanD/CEDD](https://www.pland.gov.hk/file/resources/ava_register/government/pdf/AVRG73_AVA_FinalReport.pdf)) — and adds least-cost-path ventilation corridors under a comparative AVA framing. Chapter 3 wires terrain algorithms the code already computes but never uses into a D8 fill-and-spill cascade guarded by a mass-balance assertion. Chapter 4 shows that one intervention model can drive three separate, incommensurable deltas, and Chapter 5 sets out the eight-stage build roadmap with runnable acceptance tests and standardised honesty labels.

This report is a progress document. It reports findings already established and the way forward, not a finished system.
conclusion:
The question this report set out to answer was practical: can a design-responsive heatmap, a ventilation screen and a drainage view be conducted inside a pure numpy/pillow/scipy sandbox that runs in seconds on a laptop, without CFD, GDAL or a GPU? The evidence across the five chapters says yes — but only by treating the three as **one geometry read three ways**, and only by refusing to claim more than each screen can prove.

Three moves carry most of the leverage, and Chapter 5 orders them explicitly. **First**, a single `evaluate(scenario)` must return three separate deltas — a heat delta, a wind delta and a drainage delta — never one blended score, because the three axes are incommensurable: a dimensionless index, a dimensionless area ratio and a volume in cubic metres cannot be combined without weights that no published standard supplies ([Nardo et al., 2008](https://doi.org/10.1787/533411815016)). **Second**, the wind screen must break its exact NE≡SW symmetry by computing a true oriented per-cell projected width; today the axis-aligned footprints make a NE wind and its opposite byte-identical, so the screen is blind along the prevailing NE axis that matters ([AVRG73](https://www.pland.gov.hk/file/resources/ava_register/government/pdf/AVRG73_AVA_FinalReport.pdf)). **Third**, the drainage view must add a mass-balance assertion — runoff in equals stored plus discharged — turning a global level-pool solve into a defensible D8 fill-and-spill cascade ([Barnes et al., 2021](https://esurf.copernicus.org/articles/9/105/2021/)).

The honesty position is not decoration; it is the boundary that makes the tool usable. Heat is a **relative index, not a temperature** — a hotter/cooler comparison of form and cover, never degrees Celsius. FAD is **not a velocity ratio**, and the two are never interchanged ([Ng & Cheng, 2009](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0360132308001455)). Drainage is **screening, not a flood prediction**: no pipes, culverts, outfalls, backflow or 2D dynamics ([Nobre et al., 2011](https://www.sciencedirect.com/science/article/pii/S0022169411002599)). Each output carries a machine-readable status and a human warning, following the pattern the code already uses.

The way forward is the staged roadmap of Chapter 5: eight dependency-ordered stages, each naming its files, its runnable acceptance test and its honesty label, with a frozen golden scenario guarding against regression. Some inputs remain **data-gated** rather than solved — a real bare-earth terrain from CEDD LiDAR or the Lands Department 5 m DTM, a genuine Landsat 8/9 LST scene to anchor the heat index, and the full AVRG73 wind rose in place of a single published frequency. Until those arrive the screens stay screening-level — and say so. That is the honest answer to how a design choice can be seen, in three dimensions, in seconds.
